Potpourri has two meanings — one concrete and one figurative. Both are equally valid and in common use. Understanding both will give you the complete picture of this word.
The Literal Meaning — A Physical, Fragrant Mixture

In its most original, concrete sense, potpourri is a decorative mixture of dried flower petals, herbs, spices, and plant materials, placed together in an open bowl, a jar, or a small fabric pouch. The sole purpose is to make a room smell pleasant — think of it as a natural, old-fashioned air freshener.

Typical ingredients include dried rose petals, lavender, cinnamon sticks, cloves, orange peel, and cedarwood chips. Sometimes a few drops of scented oil are added to boost the fragrance. The mixture is left out in the open so its scent slowly drifts into the surrounding air.

You would commonly find a bowl of potpourri sitting on a bathroom shelf, a coffee table, inside a wardrobe, or in a hotel lobby. It serves a double purpose — it smells good, and it also looks visually appealing because of the colorful mix of dried petals and spices.

A simple way to picture it: imagine someone collects rose petals from their garden, lets them dry in the sun, then tosses them in a bowl with some cinnamon sticks and dried lavender. That fragrant, colorful bowl is potpourri.
The Figurative Meaning — A Mixed Collection of Different Things

This is the more widely used meaning of the word, and you will encounter it far more often in books, articles, and everyday speech.

When used figuratively, potpourri means a miscellaneous assortment or mixture of many different, varied things gathered together in one place — things that may not share a single strong theme but are presented as a collection. The idea is borrowed directly from the physical object: just as a bowl of potpourri blends many different ingredients, a figurative potpourri blends many different elements.

Here are some clear examples of this meaning in use:

  • A television variety show that mixes comedy skits, musical performances, cooking segments, and celebrity interviews could be described as "a potpourri of entertainment."
  • A book containing short stories, travel essays, poems, and personal memoirs on different subjects might be called "a literary potpourri."
  • If a professor's lecture jumps from ancient history, to modern politics, to pop culture, a student might say, "Today's class was a real potpourri of ideas."
  • A music album that blends jazz, classical, folk, and electronic sounds is often described as "a potpourri of musical styles."

In every case, the word signals: "There are many different things here, and they are mixed together."
The Tone and Feeling the Word Carries

This is important to understand, because not all words that mean "a mixture" feel the same.

Potpourri carries a neutral-to-pleasant tone. The variety it describes is generally seen as interesting, rich, or even charming — not messy or chaotic. When someone calls something a potpourri, they are not criticizing the mix. They are simply acknowledging the variety, often with a hint of appreciation.

Compare this to similar words:

  • Hodgepodge — suggests a clumsy, random, somewhat messy mixture, often used critically.
  • Jumble — implies disorder and confusion.
  • Medley — similar in feel to potpourri, but used almost exclusively for music or food.
  • Potpourri — refined, pleasant, and variety-embracing in tone. It can be used in formal writing or casual speech without sounding negative.

So if a writer calls a book a "potpourri of essays," they are saying it covers many topics, and the variety itself is part of the appeal. If they called it a "hodgepodge," they might be suggesting it feels disorganized.
How Broad the Figurative Use Is

The figurative meaning of potpourri is extremely flexible. It can be applied to almost anything that consists of varied, mixed elements:

  • A playlist of songs from different genres
  • A buffet with cuisines from many different countries
  • A museum exhibition covering unrelated artists from different eras
  • A conversation that jumped between sports, politics, cooking, and childhood memories
  • A gift basket filled with chocolates, candles, books, and bath products

In all these cases, the word simply signals that there is a pleasing or notable variety — a mix of things that don't all belong to one neat category.
Knowing When Each Meaning Is Intended

Context almost always makes it clear. If someone says, "I bought some potpourri for the bathroom," they mean the physical, fragrant product. If they say, "The festival was a potpourri of art, music, and culture," they mean the figurative mixture. Because the word is most commonly encountered in its figurative sense in writing and speech, that is the meaning you should default to when you are unsure.

Potpourri is a noun with two connected meanings. First, it is a physical product — a mixture of dried flowers, herbs, and spices kept in a bowl or pouch to make a space smell good. Second, and more commonly, it is used to describe any pleasant or interesting mixture of varied, diverse things — topics, styles, ideas, or items — gathered together in one place. The word carries a warm, positive tone and celebrates variety rather than criticizing it.
